title: Comparative Analysis of Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) play a fundamental role in numerous biological processes, including gene regulation, viral replication, and RNA-based therapeutics. In recent years, deep learning approaches have emerged as powerful tools for predicting RRIs, offering improved performance over traditional computational methods. This study presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of hyperparameter optimization strategies in deep learning models for RNA-RNA interaction prediction. We evaluate prominent architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, hybrid LSTM-CNN models, attention-based Transformers, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), in conjunction with optimization techniques such as Genetic Algorithms, Bayesian Optimization, random search, and transfer learning. The comparison is conducted using benchmark RRI datasets, considering performance metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, computational efficiency, and convergence behavior. Additionally, we analyze feature representation strategies, including sequence encoding, secondary structure integration, and thermodynamic properties, and examine their interaction with hyperparameter configurations. The results highlight the strengths and limitations of different optimization strategies across model architectures, providing insights into their impact on prediction accuracy, generalizability, and training efficiency. This study serves as a guide for selecting appropriate deep learning and hyperparameter optimization frameworks for RNA interactome analysis, paving the way for more scalable and robust RRI prediction systems.

title: A Hybrid of LSTM-CNN for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are fundamental to a wide array of cellular functions, including the regulation of gene expression, RNA splicing, and viral genome replication. Accurate prediction of these interactions is essential for understanding RNA-mediated regulatory mechanisms and advancing RNA-targeted therapeutic development. In this study, we investigate a hybrid deep learning model that synergistically combines Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to enhance the prediction accuracy of RRIs. The LSTM component captures long-range dependencies and sequential context inherent in RNA sequences, while the CNN component effectively extracts local spatial patterns from sequence and secondary structure features. By integrating these complementary capabilities, the proposed hybrid model achieves improved precision and recall compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Training and evaluation were performed on benchmark RRI datasets, demonstrating superior computational efficiency and robustness. Additionally, we incorporate feature importance visualization techniques, providing interpretability and biological insights into the predictive factors driving RNA interactions. This hybrid LSTM-CNN architecture presents a powerful framework for analyzing RNA interactomes, contributing valuable tools for biomedical research and RNA therapeutics design.

title: Ribozyme Redesign From an Existing RNA Scaffold Enables Multifunctional Hydrolysis for Molecular Release.
abstract: The discovery of novel ribozymes is crucial for both advancing RNA technologies and illuminating potential RNA world scenarios. Currently, catalytic evolution of ribozymes primarily relies on the slow, random process of natural or artificial selection. In this study, we show that a distinct catalytic feature can be deliberately imposed onto a preexisting ribozyme scaffold through ribozyme redesign with a minimal alteration rather than molecular evolution. We demonstrate a single-nucleotide mutation repurposes an alkyl-transfer ribozyme into a multifunctional hydrolysis ribozyme, while preserving its overall catalytic scaffold. This hydrolase ribozyme operates analogously to a canonical protein enzyme, transforming various ester and ether substrates into the release of carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amines. Structural and kinetic analyses uncover a water-mediated mechanism for ester/ether bond cleavage. Application of this hydrolase ribozyme in living cells enables controlled activation and release of diverse payloads on demand, such as fluorescent and drug molecules, for cell-specific discrimination. This study highlights the previously underappreciated multifunctionalities within RNA catalytic architectures, broadening the scope of developing versatile ribozymes for diversified applications.

title: Large Language Models in RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: This chapter explores the transformative role of large language models (LLMs) in predicting RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs). By leveraging the sequence-based learning capabilities of LLMs, this chapter illustrates how these models can capture complex patterns in nucleotide sequences, structural motifs, and functional dependencies without explicit feature engineering. We discuss state-of-the-art architectures adapted for RNA data, including Transformer-based models and protein-inspired sequence embeddings, highlighting their performance in both supervised and self-supervised settings. Practical considerations for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs on RRI datasets are provided, alongside strategies to interpret model predictions using explainable AI approaches. Case studies demonstrate how LLMs can accelerate discovery in non-coding RNA regulation, RNA therapeutics design, and the broader transcriptomic landscape. Finally, challenges such as data sparsity, generalization to novel RNA families, and computational efficiency are examined, offering guidance for future research at the intersection of natural language processing and RNA biology.

title: Tutorial: End-to-End Deep Learning Pipeline for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: Bridging methodological advances and practical applications in computational biology requires clear, reproducible tutorials. This chapter provides an end-to-end guide for constructing deep learning pipelines for RNA-RNA interaction (RRI) prediction. Starting from raw RNA sequences, it covers dataset curation, negative sampling, feature engineering, model selection, training, evaluation, and interpretability using explainable AI techniques. Multiple modeling strategies are illustrated, including sequence-based Transformers for capturing long-range dependencies and structure-aware Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that encode secondary structures and topological relationships. Hybrid architectures integrating sequence and structural information are also demonstrated to improve predictive performance on complex RNAs. Emphasis is placed on reproducibility, with recommendations for workflow management, containerization, version-controlled datasets, and FAIR-compliant pipelines to facilitate sharing and reuse. Transparent discussion of design choices, preprocessing, and evaluation enables readers to develop robust, interpretable, and transferable RRI prediction models. This chapter equips students, researchers, and practitioners with practical tools to apply advanced deep learning to real-world RNA biology problems.

title: EWSR1 associates with the 40S ribosomal subunit and represses translation to maintain endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis.
abstract: FET family proteins (FUS, EWSR1, and TAF15) have garnered significant attention due to their involvement in oncogenic fusions and mutations in various cancers and neurodegenerative disorders. Although these highly conserved RNA-binding proteins are widely described as multifunctional regulators of gene expression, their precise molecular functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized role for EWSR1 as a selective translational repressor in cancer cells. EWSR1 specifically targets mRNAs involved in lipid metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis. Loss of EWSR1 disrupts ER morphology and impairs activation of the unfolded protein response of the ER (UPRER). Mechanistically, EWSR1 represses translation upon association with target mRNAs, and its conserved region spanning two arginine-glycine-glycine (RGG) boxes contributes to association with the 40S ribosomal subunit. These findings define a novel role for EWSR1 in post-transcriptional gene regulation and suggest that perturbations in its translational activity may underlie the pathogenesis of FET-associated diseases.

title: MitImpact 4: a genome-wide resource for the interpretation of coding and non-coding mitochondrial DNA variants.
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA variants are a frequent cause of inherited disease, yet their computational interpretation has focused almost exclusively on the 13 protein-coding genes. Variants in tRNA and rRNA genes, which carry a disproportionate share of the known pathogenic alleles, have remained a diagnostic blind spot, because their effect depends on RNA structure rather than on protein sequence and few dedicated predictors exist. MitImpact 4 removes this asymmetry. The database now covers all 49 704 single-nucleotide variants that can occur in the mitochondrial genome and reports their functional consequence, phylogenetic conservation, local mutational constraint, and population frequency in gnomAD, HelixMTdb, and ToMMo. Missense variants are annotated with APOGEE 2 and with newly added predictors, including AlphaMissense, ESM1b, VARITY, and LIST-S2, while tRNA and rRNA variants receive predictions from nAPOGEE, our RNA-specific model, alongside MitoTIP and PON-mt-tRNA. For both classes, scores are accompanied by posterior probabilities of pathogenicity that can be used within the ACMG/AMP framework for mitochondrial DNA. Clinical annotation from ClinVar and MITOMAP, including ClinGen expert-panel classifications, is integrated in a redesigned interface that also annotates user-submitted VCF files. MitImpact 4 is freely available at https://mitimpact.mcb2lab.org.

title: [RNA helicases and hematopoietic neoplasms: insights into RNA processing and disease pathogenesis].
abstract: RNA helicases comprise a large family of enzymes that act on RNA or RNA-protein complexes to remodel their structures. More than 70 RNA helicases have been identified in humans, and they are involved in nearly all cellular processes that require dynamic RNA structural rearrangements. A subset of myeloid neoplasms is associated with germline predisposition, among which DDX41, a representative member of the DEAD-box RNA helicase family, is one of the most important causative genes. Although one of the major cellular functions of DDX41 is thought to be pre-mRNA splicing, it is unlikely to directly determine splice site selection. Rather, recent studies suggest that DDX41 plays an integrative regulatory role in transcription and RNA splicing by preventing the accumulation of specific nucleic acid structures known as R-loops. This review summarizes the physiological roles of RNA helicases, including DDX41, and discusses their relevance to human disease, with a particular focus on hematopoietic neoplasms.

title: Protocols for RNA-RNA Interaction Dataset Construction and Model Training.
abstract: Protocols are central to the Methods in Molecular Biology series, enabling reproducibility and practical adoption of computational techniques. For RNA-RNA interaction (RRI) prediction, standardized protocols are essential due to the heterogeneity of data sources, preprocessing steps, and modeling choices. This chapter presents step-by-step protocols for constructing RRI datasets, generating negative samples, extracting sequence and structural features, training deep learning models, and evaluating performance through reproducible, standardized workflows. The protocols are modular and adaptable, supporting sequence-based, structure-aware, and graph-based models. By following these procedures, researchers can build robust, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR)-aligned RRI prediction pipelines suitable for both academic research and clinical applications.

title: Transformer-Based Architectures for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: The accurate prediction of RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) is a central challenge in computational RNA biology, owing to the complex, context-dependent, and long-range dependencies inherent in RNA sequences and structures. While recurrent neural networks and convolutional models have achieved notable success, they often struggle to efficiently capture global contextual relationships across long RNA sequences. Transformer-based architectures, originally developed for natural language processing, offer a powerful alternative through their self-attention mechanisms, enabling direct modeling of long-range dependencies without recurrence. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of Transformer-based models for RRI prediction, including RNABERT and biomedical adaptations of BERT, discusses RNA-specific tokenization and pretraining strategies, and examines fine-tuning approaches for interaction prediction tasks. Case studies on benchmark datasets illustrate performance gains and biological interpretability, and current limitations and future research directions are outlined.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques for RRI Prediction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) play a crucial role in regulating diverse biological processes, including gene expression, RNA splicing, and cellular signaling. Accurate prediction of these interactions is essential for understanding RNA function and advancing therapeutic design. In recent years, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques have emerged as powerful tools to model complex RNA interactions from high-dimensional and heterogeneous biological data. This chapter presents a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art ML and DL methods applied to RRI prediction. We review and analyze classical ML algorithms such as support vector machines, random forests, and ensemble approaches, alongside modern DL architectures including convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and graph neural networks. Key challenges such as feature extraction, model interpretability, and data scarcity are discussed. Furthermore, we evaluate benchmark datasets, performance metrics, and comparative studies to highlight the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. Finally, future research directions are proposed to enhance predictive accuracy and biological relevance, fostering the integration of computational predictions into experimental workflows.

title: Feature Set Analysis of RNA-RNA Interaction Dataset.
abstract: Understanding RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) is fundamental to unraveling complex biological processes, including gene regulation, RNA splicing, translation, localization, and degradation. In this work, we present a comprehensive machine learning-based feature set analysis of RNA-RNA interaction datasets to identify features that contribute most significantly to accurate interaction prediction. By leveraging diverse machine learning (ML) methods, including feature selection algorithms and explainable AI tools, we systematically analyze multiple feature categories, such as sequence composition, secondary structure, thermodynamic properties, and base-pairing probabilities. Comparative experiments using classifiers such as Random Forests (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) demonstrate that optimized feature sets improve predictive performance while reducing computational overhead. Feature importance analysis highlights biologically relevant signals, including thermodynamic stability, conserved motifs, and structural flexibility, which are critical for RNA interaction prediction. Furthermore, the integration of SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) enhances model interpretability, allowing alignment of computational predictions with biological reasoning. This work provides a thorough methodological and biological framework for RRI prediction, supporting downstream applications such as RNA-targeted therapeutics, functional annotation of non-coding RNAs, and transcriptome-wide interaction mapping. The presented pipeline serves as a robust foundation for developing interpretable, efficient, and biologically meaningful RNA-RNA interaction prediction tools.

title: Molecular Technologies for Intracellular mRNA Imaging and Their Recent Biological Applications.
abstract: Understanding the spatial and temporal behaviors of individual mRNA molecules is essential for elucidating gene expression regulation and cellular function. Imaging these processes within cells offers unique insights into transcriptional heterogeneity, mRNA transport, translation, and degradation dynamics. In this Review, we summarized the principal molecular technologies for intracellular mRNA imaging and tracking. These approaches are classified based on their compatibility with fixed cells versus live cells. Fixed-cell FISH-based methods provide spatial resolution and multiplex quantification. Live-cell systems, such as RNA stem-loop binding proteins, CRISPR/Cas platforms, fluorogenic RNA aptamers, fluorescent chemical labeling strategies, molecular beacons, and DNA circuits, enable real-time visualization of both endogenous and exogenous mRNA transcripts in live cells. We finally discuss the challenges and potential future directions for intracellular mRNA imaging. We anticipate that this Review will inspire the development of the next generation of mRNA imaging technologies in diverse biological applications.

title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.
abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Structure-Aware RNA-RNA Interaction Modeling.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are inherently structural phenomena, governed not only by linear sequence complementarity but also by secondary and tertiary folding patterns that bring distant nucleotides into spatial proximity. While sequence-based deep learning models have demonstrated promising performance, they often struggle to explicitly encode RNA structural information. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a natural and flexible framework for modeling RNA molecules as graphs, where nucleotides are represented as nodes and structural or spatial relationships are encoded as edges. This chapter presents a comprehensive treatment of GNN-based approaches for structure-aware RRI prediction. We discuss graph representations of RNA sequences and structures, graph construction strategies from predicted and experimentally derived structures, and state-of-the-art GNN architectures including Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Attention Networks, and Graph Transformers. Case studies and benchmarking results demonstrate the advantages of graph-based models in capturing long-range and non-local RNA interaction patterns. Challenges and future directions for scalable and interpretable graph-based RRI modeling are also discussed.

title: Current Trends and Future Challenges in the RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction Tools and Methods.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) continue to attract significant attention in molecular biology due to their essential roles in post-transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, and gene silencing. With the rapid expansion of sequencing technologies and computational power, a new generation of RNA-RNA interaction prediction tools has emerged, leveraging advances in thermodynamics, machine learning, deep learning, and structural biology. This chapter explores the latest trends shaping the field, including hybrid modeling approaches, integration of multi-omics data, incorporation of 3D RNA structural features, and application of graph-based learning. It also critically analyzes limitations such as model interpretability, limited ground-truth data, class imbalance, and generalizability across species. Finally, the chapter outlines key future challenges, including improving scalability, standardizing benchmarks, enhancing prediction reliability in noisy biological contexts, and increasing the accessibility of these tools for experimental validation. By identifying these opportunities and barriers, this chapter aims to provide a forward-looking roadmap for computational RRI research.

title: Triplet states of oxa- and thiamonomethine cyanines in complexes with RNA: Heavy atom effect and SASA-dependent chromophore shielding.
abstract: The triplet states of monomethine cyanine dyes (MCDs) in complexes with nucleic acids remain poorly understood, despite their fundamental importance for photochemical applications and for the design of photosensitizers. This work presents the first systematic comparative study of the triplet states of a series of unsymmetrical MCDs containing benzoxazole (oxa-) and benzothiazole (thia-) terminal heterocycles in noncovalent complexes with yeast RNA. Using flash photolysis, triplet-triplet absorption spectra and triplet decay kinetics were measured. A fundamental difference between the two groups of MCDs was discovered: thia derivatives populate the triplet state upon direct photoexcitation (with triplet quantum yields up to ~5.5%), whereas for oxa analogs, intersystem crossing is inefficient and triplets are observed only upon sensitized energy transfer. This effect is qualitatively explained by the enhancement of spin-orbit coupling upon replacement of the oxygen atom with sulfur (the internal heavy atom effect), which was confirmed by quantum chemical calculations. TD-DFT calculations have shown that the spin density of the MCD triplet state is concentrated mainly on the methine bond (with some contributions of N heteroatoms), which should be probably most susceptible to triplet quenchers. The kinetics of triplet state decay for all studied MCDs are biexponential, reflecting the heterogeneity of the RNA-binding sites. Based on the poses obtained by molecular docking, the solvent-accessible surface area of the chromophores (SASA) was calculated for each type of complexes (intercalation, groove binding, hairpin loop). A qualitative correlation between the triplet decay kinetics and SASA was shown: the "slow" component of the kinetics (hundreds of microseconds) corresponds to a strongly shielded intercalated chromophore (upon complexation, SASA decreases by ~80-85%), while the "fast" component corresponds to a chromophore localized in the groove (SASA decreases by only ~40-60%). The obtained results offer a new, structure-based approach to predicting the triplet dynamics of dyes in biopolymer microenvironments and provide a basis for the design of ligands with desired photochemical properties.

title: Tdrd9 modulates spermatogonial stem cell-associated gene expression during sex reversal in the protogynous orange-spotted grouper (Epinephelus coioides).
abstract: Tdrd9 is a conserved RNA-binding protein implicated in germ cell development, and its functional significance in teleost sexual plasticity has remained largely uncharacterized. In present study, the role of tdrd9 were investigated in the hermaphroditic protogynous orange-spotted grouper (Epinephelus coioides). Quantitative real-time PCR and immunofluorescence analyses were employed to assess spatiotemporal expression dynamics, and the expression of tdrd9 was found to be significantly upregulated during sex reversal. Subcellular mRNA and protein localization were performed to determine localization patterns, and both tdrd9 mRNA and protein were confirmed to be predominantly localized to the cytoplasm of spermatogonia in induced testis. Moreover, tdrd9 plasmids were transfected into an established grouper spermatogonial stem cell (SSC) line, and the transcriptome sequencing and Quantitative real-time PCR results of cells before and after transfection showed that piwi1 genes was upregulated, zbtb16 (plzf), and gfra1 genes were downregulated. Collectively, these findings show that Tdrd9 expression increases during sex reversal, that Tdrd9 is predominantly detected in spermatogonia, and that transient tdrd9 overexpression alters the expression of genes associated with spermatogonial maintenance and early germ cell development in SSC cells. This study provides a basis for investigating the role of Tdrd9 in male germ cell development in orange-spotted grouper.

title: LSTM-Based Methods for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are central to various biological processes, including post-transcriptional regulation, gene silencing, and viral replication. While traditional computational methods for RRI prediction rely on sequence complementarity and thermodynamic models, deep learning approaches, particularly those leveraging long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown great promise in modeling the complexity of RNA behavior. This chapter reviews recent advances in LSTM-based methods for RRI prediction, discusses the key datasets and evaluation metrics, and outlines future directions in this emerging field.

title: Chloroplast Genome Characterization and Phylogenetic Implications of Reyesia and Salpiglossis (Salpiglossideae, Solanaceae).
abstract: Solanaceae represents one of the most economically significant families among flowering plants. Genomic research within the family has primarily concentrated on some crop genera, such as Solanum L., Nicotiana L., and Capsicum L., whereas early-diverging clades remain comparatively understudied. This study presents the complete chloroplast (cp) genomes of two species belonging to the tribe Salpiglossideae (subfamily Cestroideae), Reyesia chilensis Clos and Salpiglossis sinuata Ruiz & Pav, and performs comprehensive comparative analyses across representative Solanaceae plastomes, focusing on genome structure, gene content, repeats, codon usage, nucleotide polymorphism (Pi), and phylogenetic relationships. The cp genomes of R. chilensis and S. sinuata have lengths of 156,969 and 156,262 bp, respectively, and both exhibit the characteristic quadripartite structure. Their genome organization and gene composition were highly conserved. The plastome of R. chilensis encoded 112 unique genes (111 in S. sinuata), including 79 protein-coding genes, 29 transfer RNA-coding genes (28 in S. sinuata), and four ribosomal RNA-coding genes. Comparative analyses revealed only minor sequence divergence between the two plastomes, with highly similar codon usage bias and repeat sequence composition. Phylogenetic analyses supported R. chilensis and S. sinuata as a clade representing Salpiglossideae, sister to Benthamiella patagonica Speg. (Benthamielleae), together forming an early-diverging branch within the Solanaceae. Nucleotide polymorphism analyses revealed a mean nucleotide diversity (Pi) of 0.013 within the shared genes, whereas intergenic spacers exhibited a higher sequence polymorphism (average Pi = 0.028). Several hypervariable segments were identified as promising markers for Solanaceae species delimitation and phylogenetic inference. This work contributes critical genomic datasets and further clarifies the phylogenetic comprehension across the family.

title: Biophysics-informed computational framework for predicting antisense oligonucleotide knockdown efficacy under small-data constraints.
abstract: A central strategy in treating neurodegenerative disorders, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), is lowering levels of disease-driving proteins. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) offer a direct RNA-targeted approach to reduce protein expression, but experimental discovery and optimization are constrained by small, heterogeneous datasets and target-specific variability. Computational models that predict ASO knockdown efficacy directly from sequence and context could improve candidate selection, yet generalization across gene families and experimental settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a biophysics-based computational framework for predicting RNase H-active ASO knockdown efficacy under small-data constraints. We curate and integrate heterogeneous literature-derived ASO efficacy measurements into a unified dataset and evaluate model transfer using independently generated experimental ASOs targeting ALS-relevant genes DAZAP1 and FAM69C. Knockdown efficacy is defined at the transcript level (%KD), providing a mechanistic measure of RNase H-mediated activity. To our knowledge, this is the first framework that combines ASO feature engineering with one-shot family calibration for prediction under realistic small-data conditions. We integrate sequence representations with physics-based features capturing RNA-DNA hybridization thermodynamics, targeting RNA accessibility. Compared to sequence-only baselines, this mechanistic feature augmentation reduces external wet-lab prediction error, improving generalization to independent experimental data. Despite these gains, uncalibrated predictions exhibit systematic target-family-specific scale bias. We address this challenge by using a minimal one-shot family calibration strategy that applies an additive offset derived from a single experimentally measured reference ASO per new target family. We further assess the model's behavior using a leave-one-family-out simulation on literature-derived ASO families, repeatedly applying one-shot calibration to quantify its expected benefit and variability under controlled small-n conditions. One-shot calibration markedly improves absolute prediction accuracy while preserving within-family ranking, without retraining or increasing model complexity. Out-of-distribution evaluation shows stable performance for DAZAP1 and increased uncertainty for FAM69C, consistent with the expected effects of very small sample sizes. Permutation-based interpretability analyses show that predictive signal is dominated by global sequence architecture, with thermodynamic and accessibility features providing correlated, secondary contributions. Together, these results establish a computational workflow in which literature-trained models can be transferred to new target genes using minimal experimental input, supporting systematic ASO prioritization in small-data models.

title: BacMap 3.0: a comprehensive knowledgebase of annotated bacterial genomes.
abstract: BacMap 3.0 (https://bacmap.ca) is a comprehensive, freely accessible resource integrating 23 524 bacterial and archaeal species, 32 866 genomes, >100 million genes, 1756 primary metabolic pathways, and 45 284 metabolites within one interactive platform. Despite the extraordinary growth of bacterial and archaeal genome sequencing, relevant data remain distributed across numerous specialized databases, impeding comprehensive genome-to-function analysis. While existing microbial resources generally emphasize genome annotation, taxonomy, metabolic pathways, or phenotypes separately, BacMap 3.0 unifies these complementary information layers within an organism-centred framework. It resolves this fragmentation by consolidating genomic, functional, structural, metabolic, phenotypic, ecological, and phylogenetic information into richly detailed, organism-specific "BacCards". Each BacCard combines an interactive genome map with extensive annotations covering bacterium-specific taxonomy, physiology, morphology, metabolism, protein structures, pathways, and metabolites. To facilitate data exploration, BacMap 3.0 supports taxonomic and phenotype-based browsing, chemical structure searches, interactive genome visualization, as well as gene, genome, 16S RNA, and protein BLAST searches. Building on earlier releases devoted primarily to genome visualization, BacMap 3.0 increases organismal coverage by >13-fold and transforms BacMap into an integrated bacterial knowledgebase for genome-to-function investigation across multiple biological scales. By bringing diverse biological information together in a single searchable environment, BacMap 3.0 offers a powerful platform for comparative genomics, microbiome research, infectious disease investigation, and biotechnology with a goal of accelerating the interpretation of microbial diversity, biology, and function.

title: Phagocytosis of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid- and RNA-containing immune complexes drives inflammatory cytokine production and endothelial dysfunction.
abstract: The aberrant inflammation that characterizes severe COVID-19 is incompletely understood. Given the persistence of SARS-Cov-2 RNA and nucleocapsid protein (N) and the presence of anti-N antibody during the course of severe infection, we investigated the role of RNA-containing immune complexes (ICs) in driving inflammation. We found that ICs consisting of SARS-CoV-2 RNA, N, and anti-N IgG1 are internalized by primary human monocytes and stimulate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in a manner dependent on Fcγ receptors and partially dependent on toll-like receptor-8. In addition, the inflammatory response induced in monocytes by RNA-containing ICs caused endothelial dysfunction in vascularized micro-organs. Using nasopharyngeal samples from SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals, SARS-CoV-2 RNA and N were captured by anti-N monoclonal antibody in the absence of lysing reagents, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 RNA and N complexes are present outside of virions and cells. Finally, we found that during an early wave of COVID-19, higher anti-N IgG:IgM ratios were associated with more severe clinical outcomes, consistent with a role for inflammatory, IgG-mediated phagocytic clearance of nucleic acid-containing ICs in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis, perhaps mitigated by non-inflammatory, IgM-mediated clearance. We conclude that RNA-containing ICs may play a role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19. Since all pathogenic viruses encode nucleic acid-binding proteins, such as N, and these proteins often elicit an antibody response, inflammatory clearance of nucleic acid-containing ICs may also contribute to disease severity in other viral infections.

title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor-regulated endothelial PD-L1.
abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction in Therapeutics and Drug Discovery.
abstract: RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as a transformative modality in modern medicine, enabling precise modulation of gene expression and offering new treatment strategies for previously intractable diseases. Central to the success and safety of many RNA therapeutics is a detailed understanding of RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs), including both intended target binding and unintended off-target effects. Computational prediction of RRIs plays a critical role in the design, optimization, and validation of therapeutic RNAs such as antisense oligonucleotides, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, and CRISPR-associated RNAs. This chapter examines the role of RRI prediction in therapeutic and drug discovery pipelines, highlighting computational strategies, deep learning models, and validation frameworks. Examples of applications in oncology, infectious diseases, and genetic disorders illustrate how accurate RRI modeling supports efficacy, safety assessment and contribute to evidence generation for therapeutic development. Challenges and future directions for clinically deployable RRI prediction systems are also discussed.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for RNA-RNA Interaction Models.
abstract: As deep learning models become increasingly used to RNA-RNA interaction (RRI) prediction, concerns regarding their interpretability, reliability, and biological validity have grown. High-performing models such as Transformers and Graph Neural Networks often function as black boxes, limiting their acceptance in biological discovery and therapeutic applications. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) seeks to address this challenge by providing tools and methodologies that make model predictions transparent, interpretable, and biologically meaningful. This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of XAI techniques applicable to RRI prediction models. We discuss model-agnostic and model-specific explanation methods, attention-based interpretability in Transformers and GNNs, feature attribution techniques, and biologically grounded validation strategies. Case studies from recent RRI and RNA-interaction prediction studies illustrate how explainability can highlight sequence regions, interaction sites, structural features, and other model-derived signals that can support biological interpretation and hypothesis generation.

title: Genetic Algorithm-Based Solvers for RNA-RNA Interaction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are fundamental to a wide range of cellular processes, including gene regulation, mRNA stabilization, and viral replication. Computational prediction of RRIs has traditionally relied on dynamic programming-based approaches grounded in thermodynamic models, which, although accurate, are computationally intensive and face scalability limitations when applied to large or complex RNA sequences. To address these challenges, recent research has explored alternative paradigms based on metaheuristic optimization, particularly Genetic Algorithms (GAs), which reformulate RRI prediction as an optimization problem and enable efficient exploration of large and complex search spaces. Existing studies demonstrate that GA-based methods encode RNA interaction patterns as candidate solutions and iteratively refine them using biologically inspired operations such as selection, crossover, and mutation, while integrating thermodynamic and structural constraints into fitness functions. Comparative analyses in the literature indicate that these approaches can achieve competitive accuracy with traditional methods while offering improved flexibility and scalability for large-scale and heuristic-driven RRI prediction tasks.

title: From Object Detection to RNA Interaction: Evaluating YOLOv8 and CNNs on RRI Data.
abstract: The recent convergence of computer vision and bioinformatics has opened new pathways for solving complex biological problems using deep learning. Originally developed for real-time object detection in images and videos, models like YOLOv8 (You Only Look Once, version 8) have demonstrated exceptional speed, accuracy, and generalization capabilities. This chapter investigates the adaptation of YOLOv8 and other Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures to the domain of RNA-RNA Interaction (RRI) prediction, a crucial task for understanding post-transcriptional regulation and identifying disease-associated RNA networks. We present a comprehensive evaluation of how visual and structural encoding of RNA sequences enables CNN-based models to detect meaningful patterns related to interaction potential. Emphasis is placed on model architecture, input encoding (e.g., image-like matrices from sequence/structure data), transfer learning strategies, and evaluation metrics. Our results suggest that CNNs, particularly YOLOv8 with custom-modified layers, can be effectively repurposed to learn latent spatial dependencies in biological sequences-paving the way for interpretable and scalable RRI prediction pipelines. This cross-disciplinary study underscores the power of transferring methodologies from one domain (computer vision) to another (computational biology), demonstrating promising implications for both research and clinical diagnostics.

title: Tutorial on Machine Learning Methods for RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are fundamental to numerous cellular processes, including gene regulation, RNA splicing, and translation. Accurate prediction of RRIs remains a challenging computational problem due to the complex structural and sequence dependencies involved. This tutorial and literature survey provide a comprehensive overview of machine learning (ML) methodologies applied to RRI prediction, focusing on classical models such as Naive Bayes and Bayesian networks, alongside cutting-edge deep learning techniques exemplified by Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). We explore the theoretical foundations of these methods, their feature engineering strategies, and their relative strengths and limitations in modeling RNA sequence and structural data. Through critical analysis of recent literature, this survey highlights the evolution of ML-based RRI prediction, emphasizing how probabilistic models and transformer-based architectures have advanced the field. Practical insights and guidelines for applying these methods are discussed, aiming to equip researchers with the knowledge needed to implement and interpret ML models for RNA interaction prediction effectively.

title: An Effective Pipeline to Develop Modification-Specific Intracellular Antibodies Using AI Tools.
abstract: Posttranslational protein modifications (PTMs) are often associated with protein functions. To detect PTMs in living cells, genetically encoded antibody-based probes, termed modification-specific intracellular antibodies (mintbodies), have been developed. A mintbody consists of a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of a modification-specific antibody and a fluorescent protein. By expressing mintbodies in cells or organisms, the localization and changes in the specifically modified form of a protein can be tracked in real time. In particular, mintbodies against histone and RNA polymerase II PTMs have been developed and are available. However, most mouse monoclonal antibodies fail to remain functional when expressed in the reduced environment inside eukaryotic cells due to unstable folding. This results in an inability to bind antigen, instability, aggregation, and/or degradation. Whereas there have been no general methods to develop functional intracellular antibodies, we have recently developed a convenient pipeline to efficiently convert unstable scFvs into stable and functional probes using AI-assisted tools. We here describe a practical, end-to-end protocol for converting existing antibody sequences into functional intracellular antibodies using an AI-assisted design pipeline combined with live-cell screening. The method integrates antibody sequence annotation, structure prediction, deep-learning-based framework optimization, and experimental validation in mammalian cells.

title: Targeted CPSF6 recoding reveals global fitness advantages of SPAD integration targeting and cell type-specific roles for capsid binding in HIV-1 DNA synthesis and nuclear import.
abstract: As part of the CFIm complex, CPSF6 regulates cellular gene expression via alternative polyadenylation. CPSF6 binds primate lentiviral capsids and has been implicated in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and integration targeting. However, interpretations of the role(s) of CPSF6 during HIV-1 replication are complicated by the transcriptional changes that occur when the protein is depleted from cells. To disentangle the role of CPSF6 in HIV-1 replication from alternative polyadenylation, we selectively recoded its capsid-binding phenylalanine-glycine motif to alanine-alanine in CD4-positive Jurkat T cells, CEM12D7 T cells, and THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells using CRISPR/Cas9-based homology-directed repair. While large variations in single-round HIV-1 infection were observed among isolated T cell clones, en masse comparisons of recoded T cells to cloned control T cells failed to reveal any significant differences in infection levels. Consistent with an overall fitness advantage provided by DNA integration in speckle-associated domains, which was ablated by recoding across cell types, HIV-1 replicated more robustly in control T cell populations. Single-round infection, in addition to spreading replication, was reduced in recoded myeloid/macrophage cells, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription, and more robust blocks to HIV-1 nuclear import. Recoded monocytes/macrophages, however, did not reveal any evidence for enhanced type I interferon production or sensing of HIV-1 nucleic acids. Altogether, we define endogenously recoded cell lines to uncouple capsid binding from CPSF6's role in RNA metabolism, which highlights a global fitness advantage of targeted DNA integration and cell type-specific roles for CPSF6 in HIV-1 reverse transcription, nuclear import, and virus replication proficiency.IMPORTANCEHIV-1 usurps cellular factors to effectively replicate and avoid innate immune sensing. HIV-1 capsid binds CPSF6, but the consequences of this virus-host interaction on HIV-1 biology are necessarily complicated by the cellular role of CPSF6 in pre-RNA processing. By endogenously recoding CPSF6 to selectively disrupt capsid binding while preserving its RNA-processing activity, we demonstrate in two different T cell lines that CPSF6-mediated targeting of HIV-1 DNA integration into nuclear speckle-associated domains correlates with optimal viral replication. Recoded THP-1 myeloid/macrophage cells revealed additional single-round and multi-round infection defects, which correlated with reductions in reverse transcription and HIV-1 nuclear import. These defects, however, did not correlate with enhanced type I interferon production or detection of HIV-1 nucleic acids by known innate immune sensors. Our work clarifies diverse roles for the capsid-CPSF6 interaction in HIV-1 infection of T lymphocytic versus myeloid cell lines and provides novel cell reagents for future research studies.

title: SARS-CoV-2 membrane (M) protein activates TLR4 to induce an inflammatory response.
abstract: An excessive inflammatory response, also known as "cytokine storm," is a major cause of severe COVID-19. Viral RNA and its structural proteins are key mediators of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation. While the immune sensors and host inflammatory responses induced by SARS-CoV-2 RNA and the structural proteins spike (S), envelope (E), and nucleocapsid (N) are well defined, the role of membrane (M) protein in inflammatory/antiviral response and the signaling pathway facilitating M protein-mediated immune response is not well characterized. Here, we show that SARS-CoV-2 M protein induces robust inflammatory cytokine responses in murine and human macrophages and lungs. We also show that the M protein-induced inflammatory response relies on TLR4 signaling and that MyD88 serves as the key adaptor driving inflammation, while TRIF is primarily required for the antiviral IFN response. Detailed evaluation of downstream signaling pathways highlighted the critical roles of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) molecules JNK and ERK1/2, followed by nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and p38 signaling in the M protein-TLR4-mediated inflammatory response. Finally, we show that abrogation of M protein-induced ERK1/2 and p38 signaling reduced inflammatory cytokine production and rescued type I interferon production in wild-type macrophages, while inhibition of JNK and NF-κB suppressed the M protein-induced inflammatory and antiviral cytokine responses. Collectively, our results demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 M protein induces pro-inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons via TLR4-MyD88/TRIF activation, with MAPK activation playing a dominant role, and offer specific targeting of MAPK signaling to mitigate SARS-CoV-2-induced excessive inflammation and pathology. Severe COVID-19 is often caused by an excessive inflammatory response, but the role of the SARS-CoV-2 membrane (M) protein in this process has not been well understood. We show that the M protein strongly activates inflammatory and antiviral immune responses through TLR4 signaling and identify the key signaling pathways involved. We also demonstrate that selectively targeting MAPK signaling can reduce harmful inflammation while restoring antiviral interferon responses. These findings improve our understanding of how SARS-CoV-2 causes disease and identify potential therapeutic targets to limit excessive inflammation without compromising antiviral immunity.

title: Placental small-RNA sequencing reveals a distinct microRNA signature and its functional relevance in a preeclampsia rat model.
abstract: Despite extensive investigations over the last few decades, molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of preeclampsia remain incompletely understood. Emerging evidence suggests that microRNAs (miRNAs) regulate key pathological processes in preeclampsia including endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and oxidative stress. However, a comprehensive profiling of miRNA expression has not been previously carried out. Thus, using reduced uterine perfusion pressure (RUPP) model of preeclampsia, we performed placental miRNA sequencing to identify functional relevance of abnormally expressed miRNAs. Blood pressure was measured via carotid catheterization on gestational day (GD)19. Placental small-RNA sequencing was performed using Illumina NextSeq2000 sequencer. Our analysis identified 142 differentially regulated miRNAs (40 up- and 102 down-regulated) in placenta from RUPP rats. The top upregulated miRNAs included miR-211-3p, miR-628, miR-6324, miR-363-5p, and miR-6329, while miR-3587, miR-29b-3p, miR-3556a, miR-29a-3p, and miR-21-3p were the most downregulated. Functional annotation revealed associations with immune response (miR-363, miR-21, miR-29), B-cell differentiation (miR-628), T-cell activation (miR-21), adipogenesis, and lipid metabolism (miR-211, miR-29, miR-21), and angiogenesis (miR-363, miR-21). Further, gene ontology analysis revealed significant enrichment in biological processes; regulation of transport, cell-cell signaling, and calcium-dependent exocytosis, cellular components; synaptic vesicles, perinuclear cytoplasm, and clathrin-coated vesicles, and molecular functions; glycoprotein binding, protein dimerization, and myosin binding. These findings suggest that robust miRNA dysregulation in RUPP rats may underlie disease pathogenesis.

title: METTL family proteins: functional heterogeneity, tumor regulatory networks, immune microenvironment remodeling and therapeutic potential.
abstract: RNA methylation serves as an essential post-transcriptional epigenetic modification for gene expression regulation. The methyltransferase-like (METTL) family is characterized by conserved methyltransferase domains. These members can recognize multiple RNA substrates including messenger RNA (mRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), and mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA), and engage in a variety of RNA methylation processes. They exhibit markedly heterogeneous tumor-regulatory functions. The METTL3/14 complex regulates tumor proliferation, metastasis, metabolic reprogramming and immunotherapy resistance by catalyzing mRNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification. METTL5 targets rRNA and drives translational reprogramming to participate in tumor progression and T cell immune resistance. METTL17 mediates multiple methylations of mtRNA to deregulate mitochondrial metabolism and drive malignant tumor phenotypes. METTL16 possesses both mRNA m6A catalytic and small nuclear RNA non-catalytic functions, and participates in tumor progression and immune escape. METTL4 catalyzes N6, 2'-O-dimethyladenosine methylation to modulate target gene translation and facilitate tumorigenesis. Beyond RNA methylation, METTL7A/B promotes resistance to tumor-targeted drugs via m6A-independent mechanisms of DNA binding and protein interactions. Notably, the same METTL protein yields distinct immunoregulatory effects in tumor cells, T cells, macrophages and natural killer cells, with obvious context-dependence. In this paper, we systematically summarize structural features and functions of METTL family proteins, together with mechanisms underlying their regulation of the tumor immune microenvironment. We also consolidate the research progress and transformation bottlenecks of multiple targeted candidate molecules. It provides a theoretical basis and new ideas for further investigations of METTL-based tumor immunotargeted therapy.

title: CRISPR/Cas genome editing strategies to enhance abiotic stress tolerance in sugar crops.
abstract: Sugar crops including sugarcane, sugar beets, and sweet sorghum, are fundamental for global sucrose supply and crucial feedstocks for bioethanol production and industrial bioproducts. However, yield and sucrose accumulation are significantly influenced by abiotic stresses, including drought, salinity/alkalinity, heat, chilling/freezing, and heavy metal toxicity. The polygenic complexity of stress tolerance, particularly in sugarcane with its large, polyploid, and haplotype-diverse genome, presents significant challenges for conventional breeding, rendering it slow and imprecise. This review combines advances in genome-editing technologies, including CRISPR/Cas systems (Cas9 and Cas12a), along with transcriptional techniques (CRISPRa/i), base editors, and prime editors. These tools, combined with the progress in reference genomes, haplotype-resolved assemblies, and pangenomes, have facilitated precise gene discovery, genomic selection, and targeted editing. CRISPR-based approaches offer promising avenues for enhancing key stress-responsive pathways governing oxidative homeostasis, membrane integrity, osmotic regulation, hormone signaling, and ion-homeostasis in sugar crops. Prominent candidate targets include transcription factors (TF), signaling components, raffinose biosynthesis genes implicated in freezing tolerance, regulators of salt and alkaline stress, and determinants of heavy metal tolerance and sequestration. Translational challenges, such as off-target effects, low transformation efficiencies, and editing multiple homologues or haplotypes, are being addressed such as DNA-free ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, high-throughput screening, haplotype-specific target design, and haplotype-aware guide RNA engineering based on unique genetic variation sites across different gene haplotypes. Collectively, the integration of advanced CRISPR toolkits with enhanced genomic information resources and phenotyping capabilities holds significant potential for accelerating the development of precision-bred, multi-stress-resilient sugar crops that sustain yield, quality, and industrial value under abiotic stress conditions.

title: Emerging Roles of ETV4 in Tumor Microenvironment Remodeling: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Targeting.
abstract: ETS variant transcription factor 4 (ETV4), a member of the PEA3 subfamily of ETS transcription factors, has emerged as an oncogenic transcriptional regulator that promotes tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. Although previous studies have largely focused on its cancer cell-intrinsic functions, accumulating evidence suggests that ETV4 also contributes to remodeling of the tumor microenvironment (TME). ETV4 influences diverse microenvironmental processes, including metabolic adaptation, immune crosstalk, stromal and extracellular matrix remodeling, and cellular responses to hypoxic and mechanical stress. It has also been implicated in extracellular vesicle- and non-coding RNA-mediated communication, further supporting its role in coordinating reciprocal interactions between tumor cells and their surrounding microenvironment. Collectively, these findings position ETV4 as a molecular interface linking oncogenic signaling to TME reprogramming. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on the involvement of ETV4 in metabolic, immune, stromal, extracellular matrix, hypoxic, and intercellular communication networks. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at suppressing ETV4-associated activity through inhibition of upstream RTK-MAPK signaling, disruption of transcriptional cofactor dependencies, modulation of protein stability, and targeting of ETV4-dependent microenvironmental interactions. A more comprehensive understanding of ETV4-mediated tumor-microenvironment crosstalk may uncover context-specific vulnerabilities and provide a rationale for combination therapeutic strategies in ETV4-active malignancies.

title: Nucleotide-resolution mapping of RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications and comprehensive analysis of global polyadenylation events in mRNA 3' end processing in malaria pathogen Plasmodium falciparum.
abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA, yet its distribution and potential involvement in mRNA 3'-end processing in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum remain poorly understood. Here, we combined nucleotide resolution DART-seq, Nanopore DRS, MeRIP-seq and complementary 3'-end sequencing approaches to investigate the relationship between m6A deposition and mRNA 3'-end formation across the parasite transcriptome. DART-seq identified 2,330 reproducible m6A sites in 1,195 genes, revealing stage-associated differences in the epitranscriptome and preferential enrichment of m6A within 3' UTRs. Independent MeRIP-seq analysis further supported the reproducibility of these methylation patterns. mRNA 3'-end mapping revealed that cleavage and polyadenylation frequently occur within exceptionally adenosine-rich sequence regions. Integration of Nanopore DRS-derived m6A stoichiometry with experimentally defined poly(A) sites revealed preferential m6A enrichment at canonical DRACH motifs approximately 30-50 nucleotides upstream of transcript cleavage sites. Notably, single-molecule DRS analysis demonstrated differential m6A occupancy at shared transcript positions between proximal and distal alternative polyadenylation isoforms of the same gene, with lower occupancy in distal isoforms near proximal cleavage sites. Moreover, m6A enrichment was consistently observed upstream of the utilized poly(A) site in individual transcripts, suggesting an association between m6A deposition and alternative 3'-end formation. Distinct spatial associations of RNA secondary structure and m6A with poly(A) site regions were observed. Together, these findings provide a transcriptome-wide and single-molecule view of m6A modification patterns in relation to native poly(A) sites in P. falciparum, and the data are consistent with a model in which m6A is associated with and may contribute to 3'-end processing.

title: Extending Peptide Ligation to Acidic pH and Junctions Comprising Glycosylated and Phosphorylated Amino Acids.
abstract: The native chemical ligation (NCL) is a cornerstone of protein synthesis, allowing the assembly of peptide fragments into larger proteins. Ligation auxiliaries extend the scope of NCL beyond cysteine, but fragment ligation at sterically encumbered junctions remained inaccessible. Herein, we introduce a pyridine-containing ligation auxiliary that allows NCL to proceed at virtually any junction, including reactions at β-branched amino acids, as well as O-glycosylated or O-phosphorylated amino acids. Through iteration of the auxiliary scaffold, we revealed a fundamental relationship between the basicity of the pyridine and ligation speed. Surprisingly, the 2-mercapto-2-(4,5-dimethoxypyridin-2-yl)ethyl (MDPE) auxiliary operates over a broad pH range, enabling ligations even in highly acidic conditions. This property was leveraged in the synthesis of dodeca-phosphorylated peptides from the large RNA polymerase II CTD domain. Additionally, we utilized the MDPE auxiliary for the synthesis of heavily glycosylated segments derived from mucin MUC5AC.

title: Drosophila eIF4E paralogs: a paradigm of functional divergence.
abstract: A cardinal factor in the regulation of mRNA life and function is the cap-binding protein eIF4E. eIF4E promotes the recruitment of mRNA to the ribosome during the initiation step of translation, but other activities have been described, including mRNA processing, export, and storage. To perform these functions, eIF4E must associate with the mRNA cap and a number of different eIF4E-interacting proteins (4E-IPs). Thus, eIF4E has evolved as a key interphase between RNA metabolism, gene expression, and development. In Drosophila melanogaster seven genes encode eight eIF4E cognate proteins that have functionally diverged to perform different activities. We review the structure, interactors, biochemistry, and activities of the Drosophila eIF4E paralogs, which represent a paradigm of divergence during metazoan development.

title: A sample-to-answer framework for on-site body fluid identification based on microbial signature.
abstract: On-site body fluid identification can rapidly provide decisive evidence for crime scene reconstruction and suspect apprehension. However, current laboratory-based methods are unsuited to field-based scenarios. Protein-based biochemical strategies fail to amplify trace biomolecules and protein is susceptible to denaturation, while nucleic acid-based approach relying on RNA profiling or DNA methylation inevitably requires purification, endonuclease digestion or bisulfite conversion that conflict with speediness and convenience. Therefore, a rapid, portable, and user-friendly strategy is urgently needed for on-site body fluid identification. In this study, a systematic sample-to-answer framework for on-site body fluid identification is established based on microbial signature. A tailor-made lysis buffer is formulated to lyse Streptococcus salivarius and Lactobacillus crispatus, characteristic of saliva and vaginal secretion respectively, releasing nucleic acids for direct amplification without further purification. Due to the excellent efficiency under straightforward condition, loop-mediated isothermal amplification is employed for characteristic DNA recognition. Besides, a lateral flow device is assembled, enabling result interpretation by naked eye. To suppress carryover contamination under rudimentary field conditions, uracil-DNA glycosylase-based anti-aerosol strategy is further integrated. The sole apparatus required is only a heater for isothermal incubation during amplification. Hence, a handheld device of cigarette-case size is designed and fabricated to fit this framework and on-site deployment. The reagents for amplification are mixed and lyophilized beforehand to simplify the procedure more and avoid cold-chain transport. A systematic sample-to-answer framework for on-site body fluid identification is established, enabling accurate identification of body fluid left on various carriers involving sexual assault and confinement. The entire workflow can be completed within 1 h, substantially reducing the operational complexity and equipment requirement of conventional laboratory-based assays. This framework demonstrates its feasibility as a rapid and practical tool for on-site body fluid identification and highlight its potential for field deployment in forensic investigations.

title: FTO deficiency mediates ferroptosis to exacerbate cobalt-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: Cobalt, a toxic environmental contaminant, has been implicated in human neurological damage. However, the detailed molecular basis of cobalt-triggered neurotoxicity remains poorly uncovered. In the present study, we elucidated the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) demethylase fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) downregulation mediates the activation of ferroptosis to drive cobalt-triggered neurodegeneration. We established an in vitro model using H4 cells and an in vivo model using C57BL/6 mice. Animal experiments provided initial evidence underscoring the critical involvement of ferroptosis in cobalt-associated neurotoxicity. Furthermore, in vitro assays revealed that ferroptosis is triggered subsequent to oxidative stress induced by cobalt exposure. Notably, MeRIP-seq profiling of H4 cells and mouse cortex revealed that ferroptosis-associated genes exhibited differential m6A modification, suggesting m6A modification might be involved in modulating ferroptosis. Concurrently, Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed that genes bearing differential m6A modifications were significantly clustered within pathways linked to ferroptosis as well as neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, we found that FTO depletion effectively enhanced ferroptosis following cobalt-induced oxidative stress. Mechanistically, FTO depletion enhanced m6A modification of GPX4 and transferrin receptor protein 1 (TFRC) mRNAs, leading to reduced GPX4 and elevated TFRC expression, which aggravated cobalt-induced ferroptosis. More importantly, we observed that central nervous system specific knockout of Fto exacerbated cobalt-induced neurobehavioral deficits and neuropathological damage through ferroptosis activation. Collectively, these results provide important insights into cobalt-induced neurotoxicity by targeting FTO deficiency-mediated ferroptosis and offer an innovative strategy for investigating neurodegenerative processes driven by environmental toxicants.

title: Comparison of two genetic systems for protein production in Cupriavidus necator H16.
abstract: Many chemical manufacturing routes are being replaced with enzymatic processes to improve sustainability. In biocatalysis, enzyme production is often the main bottleneck. Bacterial proteins are frequently produced using the workhorse E. coli BL21(DE3) and its derivatives. However, other bacteria with beneficial characteristics can also be engineered for this purpose. Cupriavidus necator H16 (C. necator), for example, is a Gram-negative bacterium well-known for its chemolithoautotrophic metabolism and high polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) accumulation. Previous studies have demonstrated protein production without inclusion body formation, which is one of the main challenges when producing enzymes in E. coli. Nevertheless, high-yield protein production in C. necator remains an understudied field. Here, we investigated the bottlenecks limiting protein production in C. necator. We optimized a T7 RNA polymerase genetic system and quantified the impact of several genetic elements such as T7 promoter, RBS strength and codon usage towards GFP production. Codon usage was the main factor limiting protein production in C. necator. Tuning the RBS strength and selecting a different T7 promoter strongly influenced expression leakiness. We then produced the ene-reductase YqjM from Bacillus subtilis in C. necator, analyzing the performance of the engineered C. necator strain and our previously developed pMVRha expression plasmid. C. necator produced high amounts of soluble protein and one of the strains produced higher amounts of FMN-loaded enzymes compared to E. coli BL21(DE3) in the conditions tested. This result highlights the potential of non-model bacteria to achieve high-yield enzyme production and promote the transition to biocatalysis-driven chemical synthesis.

title: A systematic delineation of 3'UTR regulatory elements and their contextual associations.
abstract: The 3'UTR encodes regulatory information that shapes transcript abundance and subcellular distribution, yet the underlying sequence rules remain incompletely defined. We quantified the effects of ∼2 million synthetic 3'UTR inserts in A549 and HCT116 cells on RNA output and nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning. We identified a broad repertoire of short 2- to 8-nt elements. Their effects largely followed a dominant coupled axis linking high RNA output with cytoplasmic enrichment and low RNA output with nuclear enrichment and were predominantly additive. A context-aware deep learning model captures most of this behavior while revealing that strong context dependence is uncommon and emerges mainly in rare, extreme contexts consistent with higher-order constraints. Applying the model to ClinVar 3'UTR variants prioritizes a subset of pathogenic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with aberrant predicted effects, frequently explained by creation or disruption of splice-site-like U1 motifs that can trigger telescripting-associated readthrough, highlighting a potent route to 3'UTR-driven disease mechanisms. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

title: Cascade signal amplification-based electrochemical aptasensor for sensitive detection of enrofloxacin in animal-derived foods.
abstract: Enrofloxacin (ENR), a broad-spectrum antibacterial agent widely used in animal husbandry, requires stringent monitoring of its residues in animal-derived foods. Herein, we present a sensitive electrochemical aptasensor for ENR detection by integrating entropy-driven catalysis (EDC) with Mg2+-dependent RNA-cleaving DNAzyme (RCD) in a functionally coupled cascade signal amplification strategy. The presence of ENR triggers the strategy, first generating RCD via the EDC reaction. Unlike conventional tandem amplifications, our design is distinguished by two key innovations. The EDC product is intrinsically engineered to serve as a directly functional RCD unit without purification or reconstitution, and the RCD cleavage is constructed as a self-regenerating cycle in which each cleavage event releases a fragment that reassembles with excess fuel strand to form a new active RCD complex. The RCD then leads to cyclic cleavage, resulting in significantly amplified electrochemical signals. The aptasensor demonstrates a wide linear range from 100 fg/mL-100 ng/mL and a low limit of detection (LOD) of 66 fg/mL. The practical performance of the aptasensor was rigorously evaluated through the detection of ENR in pork, chicken, eggs, and milk, with results showing excellent agreement with those from confirmatory HPLC-MS/MS analysis. This study contributes to food safety assurance by developing a sensitive and accurate detection platform for ENR residues in animal-derived foods.

title: Comparative screening identifies gga-miR-204 as a nutrient-responsive miRNA that targets MAP1LC3B and promotes infectious bursal disease virus replication in HD11 cells.
abstract: Infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV) is a highly contagious immunosuppressive pathogen that causes substantial economic losses to the poultry industry. Although metabolic pathways and key metabolic genes involved in viral replication have been extensively studied, systematic approaches for identifying nutrient-responsive microRNAs (miRNAs) that functionally regulate IBDV replication remain limited. In this study, amino acid- and glucose-starvation models were established in chicken HD11 macrophages and integrated with IBDV infection-associated miRNA profiling to comparatively screen for nutrient-responsive miRNAs potentially involved in viral replication. Short-term nutrient deprivation altered LC3-associated molecular phenotypes and reduced IBDV VP2 protein expression. Small RNA sequencing revealed that nutrient starvation and IBDV infection induced distinct but partially overlapping miRNA expression profiles, with predicted target genes enriched mainly in metabolic and stress-response pathways. gga-miR-204 was upregulated under amino acid and glucose starvation but downregulated following IBDV infection. Functional assays showed that gga-miR-204 overexpression increased viral RNA levels, VP2 protein expression, and infectious virus production, whereas inhibition of endogenous gga-miR-204 suppressed IBDV replication. Reporter assays supported targeting of the chicken MAP1LC3B 3' untranslated region by gga-miR-204, and mimic treatment reduced LC3-II abundance in HD11 cells. MAP1LC3B silencing increased VP2 abundance, whereas MAP1LC3B overexpression decreased it. These findings identify gga-miR-204 as a nutrient-responsive miRNA that promotes IBDV replication in HD11 cells and support MAP1LC3B as a candidate target with functional effects on VP2 abundance. Whether MAP1LC3B mediates the proviral effect of gga-miR-204 remains to be established. This comparative screening approach provides a starting point for identifying nutrient-responsive miRNAs and investigating their potential roles in linking cellular metabolic state to IBDV replication.

title: Support Vector Machine (SVM)-Based Review of RNA-RNA Interaction Prediction Methods.
abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) play a vital role in cellular processes including gene regulation, RNA editing, and translational control. Aberrant RRIs are increasingly recognized as contributors to cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis. Accurate computational prediction of RRIs therefore offers significant opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, understanding tumor biology, and therapeutic target identification. Among machine learning approaches, support vector machines (SVMs) have been applied in RRI prediction due to their robustness in handling high-dimensional, nonlinear data and relatively small training datasets. This chapter reviews SVM-based methods for RRI prediction, highlights representative tools and strategies, and discusses current challenges and relevance to cancer application. Emerging trends that integrate SVMs with deep learning and experimental data augmentation are also outlined, pointing toward pathways for clinical translation.

title: Circ_0024390 promotes renal tubular EMT through the miR-6890-3p/CHD4 axis: implications for renal interstitial fibrosis.
abstract: Renal interstitial fibrosis (RIF) is a central pathological event in the progression of various chronic kidney diseases (CKD) to end-stage renal disease, for which effective therapeutic strategies remain lacking. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of renal tubular epithelial cells serves as a pivotal mechanism driving RIF. While circular RNAs (circRNAs) have been implicated in various pathological processes, their specific roles and underlying mechanisms in the progression of RIF remain incompletely elucidated. A circRNA microarray was utilized to screen differentially expressed circRNAs in a TGF-β1-induced HK-2 cell model of renal fibrosis. Loss-of-function experiments were performed to explore the biological effects of circ_0024390 on renal tubular EMT, as well as the proliferation and migration of HK-2 cells. Mechanistic assays were further conducted to verify the competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) regulatory mechanism of circ_0024390. Circ_0024390 was significantly upregulated in the in vitro fibrosis model, specifically in TGF-β1-induced HK-2 cells. Functional studies demonstrated that knockdown of circ_0024390 effectively attenuated renal tubular EMT and inhibited key cellular processes, including proliferation and migration. Mechanistic investigations further revealed that circ_0024390 functioned as a ceRNA by sponging miR-6890-3p. This sponging relieved the repressive effect of miR-6890-3p on its downstream target, chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4), leading to the upregulation of CHD4 expression. These findings delineate a novel circ_0024390/miR-6890-3p/CHD4 axis that promotes EMT in renal tubular epithelial cells and contributes to the progression of RIF. This study provides new insights into the pathogenesis of RIF and highlights circ_0024390 as a potential promising therapeutic target for CKD.

title: Ginsenoside Rg1 Alleviates Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Partially Through Regulating ABCB1-Mediated Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
abstract: To investigate the protective effects of ginsenoside Rg1 on lung injury in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and to elucidate the underlying mechanism involving ATP-binding cassette subfamily B member 1 (ABCB1)-mediated regulation of mitochondrial function. A COPD rat model was established by cigarette smoke exposure, followed by in vivo administration of different doses of ginsenoside Rg1. ABCB1 knockdown was achieved by tail vein injection of short hairpin RNA (shRNA). Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) and Masson staining were performed to evaluate lung histopathology and collagen deposition. Pulmonary function was assessed by measuring inspiratory resistance (Ri), dynamic lung compliance (Cdyn), and the ratio of forced expiratory volume at 0.3 s to forced vital capacity (FEV0.3/FVC).
